newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-PUNCH-UPS AND DRAMA IN SOUTH AMERICAN CUP QUALIFIERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PUNCH-UPS AND DRAMA IN SOUTH AMERICAN CUP QUALIFIERS.

text.p: Police were on the field in two matches to separate brawling players as dramatic soccer and punch-ups were mixed in South America's World Cup qualifying matches on Wednesday.
Incensed Argentine players took part in a 10-minute scrap in La Paz as they crashed to a shock 2-1 defeat against Bolivia and slid to fifth place in the nine-team group.
Riot police came onto the field to stop the Argentines, several of whom were visibly wild with rage, from attacking members of the Bolivian team bench during a game which saw two Argentines sent off.

Argentine coach Daniel Passarella, who aroused local passions before the game by saying it was inhuman to play at the altitude of La Paz, later said his team would lodge a complaint with authorities. "I thought these things had been overcome in South American football," he said.
Paraguayan goalkeeper Jose Luis Chilavert and enigmatic Colombian striker Faustino Asprilla came to blows late in the clash between the group's two leading teams and were also sent off in Asuncion.
The incident led a melee involving players, both benches and police and play was delayed for five minutes. Paraguay went onto win 2-1 to go three points clear at the top.
The tension is likely to continue as Wednesday results kept the group wide open with seven games each to play. The top four countries qualify for the 1998 finals in France.

Paraguay, with 20 points from nine games and four of their remaining seven matches at home, look set to reach the finals for the first time since 1986. Colombia, with 17, also look a good bet to qualify despite suffering their second successive defeat.
Behind them, on 13 points and separated only on goal difference, are Bolivia, Ecuador, Argentina and Uruguay.
Peru, on ten points, and Chile, on nine with a game in hand, cannot be counted out especially as the latter play six of their remaining games at home.
Argentina, in the middle of an indifferent campaign, arrived in La Paz in a sulky mood, complaining bitterly about the difficulties of playing at 3,600 metres above sea level.
They still seemed to be feeling sorry for themselves as Marco Sandy gave Bolivia, whose intricate passing constantly troubled their opponents, an eighth-minute lead against a disorganised defence.

Nestor Gorosito equalised before halftime with a penalty but early in the second half Fernando Ochoaizpur, an Argentine-born Bolivian, hammered in a rebound after goalkeeper Ignacio Gonzalez saved three successive shots.

Argentina, who had been bickering constantly, then lost their heads completely. Nelson Vivas was sent off after committing two bookable offences in quick succession and he was quickly followed by Gustavo Zapata, who found time to argue with Bolivian players before leaving the pitch.
The match culminated with the brawl, which appeared to start with a row between Argentine striker Julio Cruz and members of the Bolivian team bench.
Bolivian players abandoned the pitch completely during the mayhem but were forced to hang on for a further two mintues' play after it died down.
Chilavert and Asprilla had several verbal exchanges before tempers flared in their game. The incident led a penalty from which Mauricio Serna cancelled out Carlos Gamarra's early goal for Paraguay.
But, in a dramatic match, Delis Soto slid in the winner less than two minutes later for Paraguay, who maintained a 100 percent home record.

Ecuador, who have never played in the World Cup finals, stayed in the top four by picking up their first away point, an 80th minute penalty converted by Alex Aguinaga giving them a draw with Peru in Lima.
Earlier, Roberto Palacios had put Peru in front with Nolberto Solano hitting the crossbar shortly before Ecuador equalised. Ecuador had Agustin Delgado sent off.
National anthems were not played in an effort to avoid arousing nationalist passions. The two countries were involved in a border dispute which killed dozens less than two years ago.

Twice world champions Uruguay beat Venezuela, who have only one point, 3-1 in Montevideo but with only two home games left, their hopes still look slim. They also had Paolo Montero, scorer of their second goal, sent off.
